problems.title: Parking Lot System
problems.description: Design an in-memory multi-floor parking lot that supports typed parking spots (SMALL/MEDIUM/LARGE), vehicle hierarchy (Bike/Car/Truck), ticket-based entry/exit, hourly pricing, and a pluggable allocation strategy. The system must be extensible so that new spot types (EV, handicapped) and new pricing policies (flat-rate, surge) can be added without rewriting core orchestration logic.

must_have: Multiple floors, each with a typed list of ParkingSpot (SMALL/MEDIUM/LARGE).
Vehicle hierarchy: Bike → SMALL, Car → MEDIUM, Truck → LARGE.
park(Vehicle) issues a Ticket; unpark(ticketId) vacates the spot and computes price.
Availability display grouped by floor and spot type.
nice_to_have: Multiple gates with concurrent access (ReentrantLock or synchronized block).
EV charging spots (new SpotType + strategy extension).
clarifying_questions: Should one vehicle ever occupy more than one spot? (Assume NO for V1.)
Nearest-first or first-fit allocation — does it matter to you for V1?
Is pricing hourly only, or should PricingStrategy be injected from day one?
Do gates belong in the base design, or can I call park/unpark directly on ParkingLot?
Should duplicate vehicle (same plate number) prevent re-entry?

classes.name: ParkingLot
classes.responsibility: Single orchestrator: own floors, strategies, and the active-ticket registry. Delegates allocation to ParkingStrategy and billing to PricingStrategy. Does NOT calculate pricing or search spots directly.
classes.design_notes: Apply Singleton pattern if the problem implies one shared lot. Use ReentrantLock around spot assignment to prevent concurrent double-booking at multiple gates.

classes.name: Floor
classes.responsibility: Maintain an ordered list of ParkingSpot objects for one level. Does NOT contain business rules — it is a structural container.
classes.design_notes: Keep Floor dumb. Spot-finding logic belongs in ParkingStrategy, not here.

classes.name: ParkingSpot
classes.responsibility: Represent one physical slot. Track type, occupancy, and current vehicle. Expose occupy/vacate with minimal coupling to the lot.
methods: canFit(Vehicle v) : boolean  // optional if type-matching is in strategy
classes.design_notes: Do NOT put SpotType-to-VehicleType mapping here; it couples the spot to vehicle business rules. Keep it in the strategy.

classes.name: Vehicle
classes.responsibility: Abstract base carrying licensePlate and VehicleType. Subclasses (Bike, Car, Truck) exist to model the real world and allow future per-type overrides.
classes.design_notes: Java: abstract class Vehicle, then class Car extends Vehicle. Ruby: base class with attr_reader. Truck/Bike sub-classes each call super with fixed type.

classes.name: Ticket
classes.responsibility: Immutable receipt linking a vehicle, spot, and entry timestamp. Needed by PricingStrategy to compute billing.
classes.design_notes: Created inside park(); stored in ParkingLot.activeTickets. Removed on unpark.

classes.name: ParkingStrategy (interface)
classes.responsibility: Encapsulate the allocation algorithm. Allows swapping NearestFirst, SpreadEvenly, or any future strategy without changing ParkingLot.
classes.design_notes: NearestFirstParkingStrategy: iterate floors and spots in order, return first match by SpotType. Throws ParkingLotFullException if none found.

classes.name: PricingStrategy (interface)
classes.responsibility: Encapsulate billing logic. HourlyPricingStrategy computes price from ticket entry time to now. Swap in FlatRatePricingStrategy or SurgePricingStrategy without touching ParkingLot.
classes.design_notes: HourlyPricing: use Duration.between(entryTime, now()).toHours() × rate. For interview, you can hardcode rate=10.0 and note it is configurable.

relationships: ParkingLot 1..* Floor  (composition — floors die with lot)
ParkingLot depends on ParkingStrategy  (injected, not owned)
ParkingLot depends on PricingStrategy  (injected, not owned)
Ticket 1..1 ParkingSpot  (association — spot snapshot at entry)

design_patterns.name: Strategy
design_patterns.why: Both allocation and pricing are volatile policies. Without Strategy, adding a new algorithm forces edits to ParkingLot (OCP violation). With Strategy, you new NearestFirstParkingStrategy() and inject — zero changes to the orchestrator.
design_patterns.signal_phrase: I am separating allocation and pricing into strategies so the lot doesn't need to change when we add flat-rate weekends or EV-only spots.

design_patterns.name: Singleton
design_patterns.applied_to: ParkingLot instance (optional but common interview shorthand)
design_patterns.why: A real parking lot is one physical entity; making the Java class a Singleton mirrors that reality and avoids accidental multi-instance ticket conflicts. Always mention: in production I would use DI instead of static getInstance().
design_patterns.signal_phrase: I am using Singleton as an interview shorthand because there is physically one lot. In production I would inject ParkingLot through the DI framework.

design_patterns.name: Factory
design_patterns.why: VehicleFactory.create(type, plate) hides the constructor branching. Useful if the interviewer mentions a factory or you want to show knowledge of the pattern.
design_patterns.signal_phrase: I could add a VehicleFactory to centralise subclass construction, but for now new Car(plate) is readable enough.

design_patterns.name: Template Method (implicit)
design_patterns.why: Vehicle defines the shared contract (getType, getLicensePlate) and subclasses supply the fixed VehicleType. This is Template Method in miniature.
design_patterns.signal_phrase: Vehicle forces a consistent API — any new vehicle type just supplies its type constant and nothing else.

implementation_order: 1. Enums — VehicleType {BIKE, CAR, TRUCK}, SpotType {SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE}
3. Vehicle abstract class + Bike / Car / Truck subclasses
9. ParkingLot — park(), unpark(), displayAvailability() + optional Singleton
10. Demo driver: init floors → init lot → park bike/car/truck → display → unpark → reprice
key_phrases: I will keep persistence and payment integration out of scope and focus on an extensible in-memory core.
ParkingLot should orchestrate — it should not absorb allocation logic, pricing rules, or notification concerns.
If the interviewer adds EV charging spots later, that change is localised to a new SpotType enum value and a new allocation strategy — ParkingLot itself stays untouched.
The ReentrantLock around spot assignment prevents two concurrent gate threads from giving the same spot to two vehicles.
I am using Singleton as an interview shorthand; in production I would inject ParkingLot via a DI container.
gotchas: SOLID violation: Putting vehicle-to-spot mapping inside ParkingSpot or ParkingLot directly (SRP + OCP break). Put it in the strategy.
SOLID violation: God-class ParkingLot that calculates price, finds spots, manages exceptions AND sends notifications — extract each concern.
Bug: Forgetting to vacate() the ParkingSpot when unparking — spot stays occupied forever.
Bug: Not removing the ticket from activeTickets on unpark — ticket remains valid for a second free exit.
Edge case: Duplicate vehicle (same plate) already inside — check activeTickets by licensePlate before issuing new ticket.
Edge case: Invalid ticket ID on unpark — always throw InvalidTicketException, never silently ignore.
Design flaw: Hard-coding SpotType→VehicleType mapping as string comparisons instead of enum relationship.
Performance note: NearestFirst is O(floors × spots). Mention that a PriorityQueue of available spots per SpotType brings it to O(log n) — but O(n) is fine for the interview.
framework.extensibility_test: Interviewer says: 'Add EV charging spots and priority handicapped parking.' Walk through: (1) Add EV and ACCESSIBLE to SpotType enum, (2) Add HANDICAPPED_VEHICLE to VehicleType, (3) Create AccessibleParkingStrategy that checks permit flag on Vehicle before assigning spot, (4) ParkingLot gets new strategy injected — zero change to its core logic. This demonstrates OCP, Strategy, and DIP all in one answer.

clarify: State that persistent storage and payment gateway are out of scope upfront — this saves 5 minutes of dead-end discussion.
Ask: 'Is first-fit allocation acceptable for V1 or do you want nearest-spot optimisation?' — this positions you as thinking about trade-offs.
Call out duplicate vehicle and invalid ticket as the two primary error paths you will handle.
Decide on concurrency stance: 'I will mention thread-safety with a ReentrantLock and note it as a concern without over-engineering it.'
model: Start with the noun-from-requirements technique: ParkingLot, Floor, ParkingSpot, Vehicle, Ticket are all nouns in the problem statement.
Model VehicleType and SpotType as enums immediately — never as raw strings.
ParkingLot OWNS its floors (composition). Strategy and PricingStrategy are INJECTED (dependency inversion).
Ticket is the join entity between a Vehicle and a ParkingSpot at a point in time — include entryTime for billing.
design: Introduce ParkingStrategy and PricingStrategy interfaces BEFORE writing any implementations. Explain WHY (OCP, DIP, replaceability).
Name your exceptions first: ParkingLotFullException and InvalidTicketException. Custom exceptions are a signal of maturity.
Explicitly say: 'ParkingLot is an orchestrator, not a pricing engine or a spot-finder. It delegates both concerns.'
Optional: mention Singleton with the caveat about DI in production.
implement: Code in this exact order: enums → exceptions → models (Vehicle hierarchy, ParkingSpot, Floor, Ticket) → interfaces (ParkingStrategy, PricingStrategy) → implementations → ParkingLot → Demo.
NearestFirstParkingStrategy: nested loop over floors then spots. mapVehicleToSpotType() is a private helper inside the strategy — keeps the mapping in one place.
In park(): lock → findSpot → spot.park(vehicle) → create Ticket → activeTickets.put → return Ticket.
In unpark(): get ticket → spot.vacate() → compute price → activeTickets.remove → return price.
review: Edge case: Duplicate vehicle on entry — check if plate exists in activeTickets values before assigning new spot.
Concurrency: 'At multi-gate scenarios, two threads could assign the same spot. My ReentrantLock ensures only one thread does spot assignment at a time.'
Extensibility answer: 'EV spots → add SpotType.EV, add EVParkingStrategy, inject it. Zero change to ParkingLot or Floor.'
Performance: 'NearestFirst is O(n) where n = total spots. For scale, I would maintain a PriorityQueue<ParkingSpot> per SpotType per floor, making allocation O(log n).'

checkpoints: Must-haves and out-of-scope are explicit before drawing any class.
Vehicle-to-SpotType mapping is type-safe (no string comparisons).
ParkingStrategy and PricingStrategy interfaces exist BEFORE their implementations.
ParkingLot only calls strategy.findSpot() and pricing.calculatePrice() — it does not contain those algorithms.
park() and unpark() both handle their primary error paths (full lot, invalid ticket).
Demo driver shows park → display → unpark → reprice as a runnable sequence.

interview.opening_prompt: Design a parking lot system that supports multi-floor parking, typed spots for bikes/cars/trucks, ticketing, and pricing. Before you name a single class, tell me what you are leaving out of scope and what the two most important error conditions are.
evaluation_rubric: Requirement scoping: Does the candidate explicitly bucket must-haves and out-of-scope before touching any design?
Entity modeling clarity: Are Vehicle, ParkingSpot, Floor, and Ticket named with the right ownership boundaries?
Strategy abstractions: Are ParkingStrategy and PricingStrategy introduced as interfaces before any implementation?
FIT rules: Is VehicleType→SpotType mapping type-safe and located in the strategy, not scattered?
Error paths: Are ParkingLotFullException and InvalidTicketException explicit custom exceptions?
Extensibility proof: Can the candidate add EV spots without touching ParkingLot?
probing_questions: Why did you choose to put the vehicle-to-spot mapping inside the strategy instead of inside ParkingSpot?
What happens if two gate attendants try to park vehicles at the exact same moment?
How would you change this design if the pricing needed to vary by time of day?
Walk me through the exact sequence of method calls from a car arriving at the gate to the ticket being issued.
If I told you we now need 50% priority spots for electric vehicles — what is the minimum code change?

sections.heading: Why Strategy Pattern is Non-Negotiable Here
sections.content: Without Strategy, every new pricing policy (flat-rate, surge, member discount) requires editing ParkingLot.unpark() — an OCP violation. Without Strategy for allocation, adding EV-only spots requires adding an if-else inside park() — again an OCP violation. Strategy = the interviewer's first check for extensibility reasoning.

sections.heading: The Lock Dilemma
sections.content: Two threads (two gates) executing findSpot() concurrently will both see the same free spot. Thread A calls spot.park(vehicle1) first, then Thread B also calls spot.park(vehicle2) — one car has no spot. Fix: ReentrantLock.lock() before findSpot, unlock in finally. Mention ConcurrentHashMap for activeTickets (safe reads at all times). Say: 'I am aware this is a simplification; at scale I would use a distributed lock or a seat-reservation pattern with optimistic locking.'

sections.heading: The Fit Rule Placement Problem
sections.content: Where does Vehicle→SpotType mapping live? BAD: Inside ParkingSpot (spot knows too much about vehicles). BAD: Inside ParkingLot (God class). CORRECT: Inside NearestFirstParkingStrategy, in a private mapVehicleToSpotType() helper. This is the Strategy owning its own logic. When you add EVParkingStrategy, it can have a completely different (or override-based) mapping.

sections.heading: Ticket as the Join Entity
sections.content: Ticket is classically a join table in relational design — the bridge between Vehicle (the owner) and ParkingSpot (the resource) at a specific instant. It carries entryTime which is the key piece of data needed by PricingStrategy. Without Ticket, unpark() has no way to know when the vehicle entered.

sections.heading: Singleton — Use Deliberately, Justify It
sections.content: Singleton is fine for this problem IF you justify it: 'A real parking lot is one physical entity; I am reflecting that in code.' The red flag is using Singleton everywhere without justification. Always add the caveat: 'In production I would inject this through a DI container instead of getInstance().'

common_interview_dialogues.interviewer: Can you walk me through how a Car parks?
common_interview_dialogues.ideal_response: Sure. The caller creates new Car('KA-01') and calls parkingLot.park(car). Inside park(), we lock first to prevent concurrent spot conflicts. Then strategy.findSpot(CAR, floors) is called — NearestFirstStrategy maps CAR to MEDIUM spot type and iterates floors floor by floor, spot by spot, returning the first free MEDIUM spot. spot.park(car) marks it occupied. We generate a ticket ID, create Ticket(id, car, spot), store it in activeTickets, unlock, and return the Ticket. The caller keeps the Ticket for exit.

common_interview_dialogues.interviewer: What if two cars try to park at the same time?
common_interview_dialogues.ideal_response: That is the concurrent gate problem. Without a lock, both threads could see Spot 101 as free, both call spot.park(), and one car ends up without a spot. My ReentrantLock around findSpot + park ensures only one thread does this atomic operation at a time. In a distributed environment I would use a distributed lock (Redis SETNX) or an optimistic locking strategy with a version field on ParkingSpot.

common_interview_dialogues.interviewer: How do you add EV charging spots?
common_interview_dialogues.ideal_response: Three localized changes: (1) Add EV to SpotType enum, (2) Add new EVParkingStrategy that maps EVVehicle→SpotType.EV with an additional is-charger-available check, (3) Inject the new strategy into ParkingLot. ParkingLot code, Floor code, ParkingSpot code — none of them change. This is OCP in practice.

complexity_analysis.park_time: O(F × S) where F = floors, S = spots per floor — NearestFirst linear scan. O(log n) with PriorityQueue<ParkingSpot> per type.
complexity_analysis.space: O(F × S) for spot storage + O(T) for active tickets where T = parked vehicles.

deep_dive.java_full_reference: The complete annotated Java implementation is in swe-mastery-journal/LLD/code/01-parking-lot/java_demo/ParkingLotDemo.java — use it as the gold-standard reference for interview implementation order and comment quality.
deep_dive.ruby_reference: The Ruby implementation is in swe-mastery-journal/LLD/code/01-parking-lot/ruby/parking_lot.rb — shows how Strategy and Singleton translate to Ruby duck-typing and the Singleton module.
